title: From Chicago to Hudson Yards: Michelin-Starred Indienne Brings a Triple Threat of Indian Dining to Manhattan
excerpt: Chef Sujan Sarkar returns to New York with his celebrated tasting-menu restaurant, a Sanskrit-inspired cocktail bar, and a British-Indian chophouse — all under one roof.
body:
As the Indian fine-dining scene in America continues its remarkable ascent, one of its most ambitious chapters opened on May 28 in an unlikely corner of Manhattan: the second floor of Henry Hall, a luxury residential tower in Hudson Yards.

Chef Sujan Sarkar's Indienne — the Michelin-starred tasting-menu restaurant that earned its star within a year of opening in Chicago's River North neighbourhood in 2022 — has made the leap to New York. And it did not come alone. Alongside the 34-seat flagship, Sarkar is launching two additional concepts that together form one of the most comprehensive Indian hospitality ventures the city has ever seen.

## A Homecoming With a Clearer Vision

For Sarkar, the move is deeply personal. His first major break in New York came with Baar Baar, a contemporary Indian gastrobar in the East Village that he established in 2017. The restaurant introduced adventurous diners to modern Indian cuisine at a time when the city's Indian food scene was still largely defined by curry houses and buffet lines.

Since then, Sarkar has built an itinerant empire spanning Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Chicago — creating concepts including Swadesi, Sifr, and NADU before settling into Indienne's refined tasting-menu format.

"It's always been a very special place for me in New York," Sarkar said. "Coming back with Indienne — and introducing two new concepts alongside it — feels like both a homecoming and a new beginning."

## The Tasting Menu: Chaat to Seasonal Courses

Indienne's New York iteration will continue its signature multi-course format, with three nine-course tasting menus offering non-vegetarian ($195), vegetarian ($175), and vegan ($175) paths. The experience opens with chaat-inspired bites before progressing into seasonal courses that highlight layered spices, varied textures, and regional Indian influences drawn from Sarkar's upbringing.

The wine programme, developed by Chris Farrell, includes both signature and spirit-free pairing options. A sustainability-focused cocktail programme recycles ingredients from the kitchen, reflecting a growing consciousness in high-end Indian dining about waste and sourcing.

## Two More Concepts: Apas and Elder

Flanking Indienne is Apas, a high-end cocktail bar whose name derives from the Sanskrit word for water. The bar is designed as both a complement to the restaurant and a standalone destination, offering a global journey through South Asian flavours and botanicals with an emphasis on balance, subtlety, and creativity.

The third concept, Elder, is perhaps the most intriguing. A British-Indian chophouse inspired by the centuries of culinary cross-pollination between London and the subcontinent, it takes its name from elderflower — a plant woven into both British and South Asian culinary traditions. The menu centres on dry-aged meats, seafood, and sauces incorporating Indian spices and aromatics, with tableside dessert service adding a theatrical flourish.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 800,000-strong Indian-American population in the New York metropolitan area, Indienne's arrival is more than another restaurant opening. It represents the maturation of Indian cuisine in America from a comfort-food category into a fine-dining force that commands Michelin-level respect — and Michelin-level prices.

The interiors, designed in collaboration with MAPA Mueller, blend warmth and sophistication with textured finishes, sculptural lighting, and blush-toned seating. Chicago-based artist Ken Andjulis contributed Holi-inspired paintings, anchoring the space in Indian visual culture without resorting to cliche.

## What's Next

With Indienne, Apas, and Elder all set to open this summer at Henry Hall, Sarkar's triple launch could set a new template for how Indian hospitality scales in America — not through replication, but through diversification. For a cuisine that has spent decades fighting the "cheap curry" stereotype in the West, that may be the most important course of all.
